summary: Documents tracing and non-blocking, or bypass, requirements for Open Pluggable Edge Services. Tracing lets endpoints learn which services touched their data, and bypass lets them avoid a service.

plainLanguage.summary: OPES (Open Pluggable Edge Services) lets the program that sends a message and the program that receives it hand the message to other programs that can examine and change it. RFC 3897 sets out two requirements for that arrangement: the changed programs must record what they did in a trace that travels with the message, and the receiver must be able to send a request asking named services to step out of the way.

questions: how do services identify themselves in opes
subtitle: How an edge service says what it did to your message, and how you can tell it to step aside.

tldr.problem: When other programs in the network look at an application message and change it, the two ends of the conversation have no agreed way to find out who did what, and no way to get the original content back when one of them is broken.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out requirements for two features: tracing, where each entity records itself in a trace carried with the message, and bypass, where a request naming services by URI travels back through the flow asking them not to run.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that defines no encoding of its own. It says the trace and the bypass instruction are protocol extensions that each application protocol has to define, and it lists the ways each feature can be abused.

facts.label: OPES System trace entry
facts.value: MUST add its entry to the trace

facts.label: OPES processor trace entry
facts.value: SHOULD add its entry to the trace

today: RFC 3897 is an Informational memo published in September 2004, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It records requirements for two features of the OPES architecture defined in RFC 3835, and it leaves the encoding of the trace and the bypass instruction to separate application protocol documents.

sections.title: What OPES Is
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) architecture, specified in RFC 3835, enables cooperative application services between a data provider, a data consumer, and zero or more OPES processors. The application services under consideration analyze and possibly transform application-level messages exchanged between the data provider and the data consumer.

RFC 3897 documents tracing and bypass functionality for that architecture. The architecture document requires that tracing is supported in-band, which means the trace travels inside the application message rather than in a separate channel. That design goal limits the type of application protocols that OPES can support, and the details of what a trace record can convey depend on the choice of the application level protocol. For those reasons the memo documents only the requirements for OPES entities that are needed to support traces and bypass, and leaves the encoding of the two features to be application protocol specific. Separate documents are to address HTTP and other protocols. The architecture does not prevent implementers from developing out-of-band protocols and techniques for tracing and bypass, but such protocols are out of scope here.
sections.plainLanguage: OPES is a way for a message to pass through extra programs on its way across the network. Those programs can look at the message and change it. This memo covers two things those programs must do: write down what they did, and be willing to step aside when asked.

sections.title: The OPES System
sections.content:
The memo defines an OPES System as the set of all OPES entities authorized by either the data provider or the data consumer application to process a given application message. This definition is what makes clear what can be traced, or bypassed, in an OPES flow.

The nature of the authorization agreement determines whether authority delegation is transitive, meaning whether an authorized entity is authorized to include other entities. If specific authority agreements allow for re-delegation, an OPES system can be formed by induction. It starts with entities directly authorized by a data provider, or a data consumer, application, and then includes any OPES entity authorized by an entity that is already in the OPES system. Authority delegation is always viewed in the context of a given application message.

An OPES System is defined on an application message basis. Having authority to process a message does not imply being involved in processing it, so some members of the system may not take part in processing a message at all, and some members may process the same message several times. The definition also implies that there can be no more than two OPES systems processing the same message at a given time, one on the client side and one on the server side, based on the assumption that a given application message has a single data provider and a single data consumer.

The memo's example is a Content Delivery Network delivering an image on behalf of a busy web site. The OPES processors and services that the CDN uses to adapt and deliver the image make up an OPES System. In a more complex case, the OPES System also contains third party OPES entities that the CDN engages to perform adaptations, for example to adjust image quality.
sections.plainLanguage: An OPES System is the group of programs that are allowed to handle one particular message. The group is set by who authorized them, and the authorization is judged for that message alone. A program may be allowed to handle the message without actually handling it, and one program may handle the same message more than once.

sections.title: Tracing Requirements
sections.content:
An OPES trace is application message information about the OPES entities that adapted the message. OPES tracing is the process of creating, manipulating, or interpreting an OPES trace. The definition of a trace assumes in-band tracing, and the memo notes that this dependency can be removed if desired. Tracing is performed on a per message basis, the format of the trace depends on the application protocol being adapted, and a traceable entity can appear multiple times in a trace, for example every time it acts on a message.

There are two distinct uses of OPES traces. First, a trace enables an end to detect the presence of an OPES System. Such an end should be able to see a trace entry, but does not need to be able to interpret it beyond identifying the OPES System and locating certain required OPES-related disclosures. Second, the OPES System administrator is expected to be able to interpret the contents of an OPES trace. The trace can be relayed to the administrator by an end without interpretation, as opaque data such as a TCP packet or an HTTP message snapshot, and the administrator can use it to identify the participating OPES entities and the applied adaptation services, along with other message-specific information. Because administrators have various ways of looking into tracing, they require the freedom in what to put in trace records and how to format them. At the implementation level, an OPES entity involved in handling the corresponding application message is traceable, or traced, if information about it appears in that trace. The memo does not specify any order to that information: the order can be OPES System specific or defined by application bindings documents.

The entities have different levels of traceability requirement. An OPES System MUST add its entry to the trace, an OPES processor SHOULD add its entry, and an OPES service MAY add its entry. An OPES entity MAY delegate the addition of its trace entry to another OPES entity, for example an OPES System can have a dedicated OPES processor for adding System entries, or an OPES processor can use a callout service to manage all OPES trace manipulations, since such manipulations are themselves OPES adaptations.

When an OPES System forms its trace entry it MUST include its unique identification, where the uniqueness scope is all OPES Systems that may adapt the message being traced. It MUST define its impact on inter- and intra-document reference validity, and it MUST include information about its privacy policy, including the identity of the party responsible for setting and enforcing the policy. It SHOULD include information that identifies, to the technical contact, the OPES processors involved in processing the message. It MAY use a single URI to identify a resource containing several required items, for example a web page carrying a reference to the System privacy policy and the technical contact information. The memo does not define the meaning of privacy policy, policy enforcement, reference validity or technical contact, and sets no requirements on their encoding, language or format. An OPES processor SHOULD add its unique identification to the trace, with the uniqueness scope being the OPES System containing the processor. In an OPES system it is the task of an OPES processor to add trace records to application messages, and the OPES System administrator decides if and under what conditions callout servers may add trace information to application messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A trace is a record carried inside the message that names the programs that changed it. The end that receives the message only has to be able to see that a trace is there and find the required disclosures inside it. The system administrator is the one who reads the details, and the administrator may be handed the trace unread, as raw bytes.

sections.title: Bypass Requirements
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board's recommendation (3.3) in RFC 3238 requires that the OPES architecture does not prevent a data consumer application from retrieving the non-OPES version of content from a data provider application, provided that the non-OPES content exists. It suggests that the non-blocking feature, which the memo calls bypass, be used to bypass faulty OPES intermediaries once they have been identified by some method.

What counts as non-OPES content is provider dependent. The availability of non-OPES content can be a function of the internal policy of an organization that has contracted the services of an OPES provider. The memo's example: Company A has a contract with an OPES provider to perform virus checking on all e-mail attachments. An employee X of Company A can issue a non-blocking request for the virus scanning service, and the request could be ignored by the OPES provider, since it contradicts its agreement with Company A. The meaning of OPES versus non-OPES content is assumed to be determined through agreements between the OPES provider, the data provider and/or the data consumer, and the agreement determines what OPES services can be bypassed and in what order.

To bypass the service for a given application message in an OPES flow means to not invoke the service for that application message. A bypass URI that identifies an OPES system or processor matches all services attached to that OPES system or processor. Bypassing of OPES processors and OPES Systems themselves requires non-OPES mechanisms and is out of scope. A bypass request is an instruction to bypass, usually embedded in an application message. If an OPES processor does not know for sure that a bypass URI does not match its service, it must bypass that service. If no non-OPES content is available without the specified service, the bypass request for that service must be ignored, so the OPES version of the content is provided instead. The memo is explicit about the consequence: it may not be possible to detect non-OPES content existence, or to detect violations of bypass rules, in environments where the tester does not know whether non-OPES content exists. The design assumes that most bypass requests are intended for situations where serving undesirable OPES content is better than serving an error message because no preferred non-OPES content exists.

The primary purpose of the bypass feature is to get usable content in the presence of service failures, and not to give the content consumer more information about what is going on; the OPES trace is for that instead. Related features exist, such as bypass service or generate an error, and bypass OPES entity or generate an error, which are useful for debugging broken OPES systems and may be defined in other OPES specifications.

In the general case a bypass request is viewed as a bypass instruction that contains a URI identifying an OPES entity, or a group of OPES entities, that perform a service or services to be bypassed. An instruction may contain more than one such URI, and a special wildcard identifier can be used to represent all possible URIs. In an OPES flow a bypass request is processed by each involved OPES processor: the processor examines the bypass instruction and, if non-OPES content is available, bypasses the indicated services. The request is then forwarded to the next OPES processor in the flow, which handles all bypass requests regardless of the previous processor's actions, and the processing chain continues throughout the whole set of processors involved in the flow.

Bypass requests are generally client centric, meaning they are originated by the data consumer application, and they go in the opposite direction to tracing requests. The bypass feature must be performed in-band as an extension to an application specific protocol, and non-OPES entities should be able to safely ignore these extensions. An OPES System MUST support a bypass feature, meaning that it bypasses services whose URIs are identified by an end, and it MUST provide the OPES version of the content if the non-OPES version is not available. An OPES processor SHOULD be able to interpret and process a bypass instruction, including one that identifies services unknown to the recipient, and it MUST forward the bypass request to the next application hop provided the next hop speaks an application protocol with OPES bypass support. A recipient of a bypass instruction with a URI that does not identify any known-to-recipient OPES entity MUST treat that URI as a wildcard identifier, meaning bypass all applicable services. In an OPES system it is the task of an OPES processor to process bypass requests, and the OPES System administrator decides if and under what conditions callout servers process them.
sections.plainLanguage: Bypass is a request that travels back through the flow, asking named services to be left out. Each program in the path looks at the request, steps aside if it can, and passes the request on. If the original content is not available without that service, the request is ignored and the altered content is sent instead, so the user gets something rather than an error.

sections.title: Protocol Binding and Compliance
sections.content:
The memo does not define how the trace or the bypass instruction is written down. The task of encoding tracing and bypass features is application protocol specific, and separate documents are to address HTTP and other protocols. Those documents must address the ordering of trace information as needed.

Compliance is defined for four subjects: the OPES System, processors, entities and callout servers. A compliance subject is compliant if it satisfies all applicable MUST and SHOULD level requirements. To satisfy a MUST level requirement means to act as prescribed by it, and to satisfy a SHOULD level requirement means either to act as prescribed or to have a reason to act differently. A requirement applies to a subject if it instructs that subject. Informally, compliance with the document means that there are no known MUST violations, and that all SHOULD violations are conscious. Compliance claims are expected to be accompanied by a list of unsupported SHOULDs, if any, in an appropriate format, explaining why the preferred behaviour was not chosen.

Only the normative parts of the specification affect compliance. Those are the parts explicitly marked using the word normative, the definitions, and phrases containing unquoted capitalized keywords from RFC 2119. Examples and illustrations are not normative. The memo also records that it contains no IANA considerations of its own, though application bindings may contain application-specific ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the trace and the bypass request ride inside an application message, the application protocol has to say what they look like. The memo lists who has to obey which requirement, and it explains that a SHOULD is not optional: a program that does not follow one has to say why.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo points to RFC 3837 for the security considerations of OPES and to RFC 3838 for the policy and authorization issues, and then adds the risks specific to the two features it defines. Both tracing and bypass are implemented as protocol extensions, so inadequate implementations may defeat safeguards built into the OPES architecture, and either facility can become a target of attacks on an OPES System. The threats are application level threats in an OPES flow, and they can affect the data consumer and the data provider application.

For tracing, because the trace information is a protocol extension, traces can be injected into the data flow by non-OPES entities. A non-OPES proxy can add fake tracing information in the form of wrong, unwanted, or non existent services, and a non-OPES entity can inject large size traces that may cause buffer overflow in a data consumer application. The same threats arise from compromised OPES entities, and from bad implementations of the tracing facility in trusted OPES entities. Compromised trace information can be used to launch attacks that give the impression that unwanted content transformation was performed, by inserting wrong entity identifiers, and it can affect entities that use message header information to perform services such as accounting, load balancing, or reference-based services. It can also be used to launch denial of service attacks that overwhelm a data consumer application or an OPES entity. Inserting wrong tracing information can complicate the debugging work of a system administrator. As a precaution, the memo says OPES entities ought to be capable of verifying that inserted traces were performed by legal OPES entities, which can be done as part of the authorization and authentication phase, with policy indicating what trace information can be expected from a peer entity.

For bypass, non-OPES entities can insert bypass instructions into the OPES flow. A non-OPES proxy can add a bypass instruction that bypasses legitimate OPES entities, and the attack might result in overwhelming the original content provider servers, since it effectively bypasses any load balancing technique. That is in effect a denial of service attack, because a legitimate data consumer application may then be unable to access some content. Since an OPES flow may include non-OPES entities, it is susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks, in which an intruder injects bypass instructions into the data path, affecting content availability or disturbing load balancing. Inconsistent or selective bypass is also a threat: one end can try to bypass a subset of OPES entities so that the resulting content is malformed and crashes or compromises the entities that process it, and such exceptions are often not tested, because implementers do not expect a vital service to disappear from the processing loop. Systems that implement access controls through OPES entities may be incorrectly configured to honour bypass and so give unauthorized access to intruders. Tap bypass is a threat in the same way: systems that implement wiretaps through OPES entities may be incorrectly configured to honour bypass and so leave undetected traffic that should have been tapped or logged, and one end can bypass services such as virus scanning at the receiving end, which hackers can use to inject viruses through the network. Following the IETF policy on wiretapping in RFC 2804, the OPES communication model does not consider wiretapping requirements, but the memo says the documented threat is real, not obvious, and that users operating in wiretapping or similar logging environments should be aware of it.
sections.plainLanguage: Both features travel inside the message, so anyone in the path can write into them. A fake trace can make it look as though content was changed when it was not, and a fake bypass instruction can push all the traffic onto the origin server, or slip a message past a virus check. The memo's advice is that each entity should check that a trace came from a legitimate one.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE: A MESSAGE PASSING THROUGH AN OPES FLOW

messages.label: MESSAGE
messages.note: The application level message enters the OPES flow at the data provider.

messages.label: MESSAGE + TRACE
messages.note: The processor analyses and possibly transforms the message, and adds its own entry to the trace carried with it.

viz.caption: WHO MUST, SHOULD AND MAY WRITE A TRACE ENTRY

items.title: OPES System
items.text: MUST add its entry to the trace, with its unique identification, its impact on reference validity, and information about its privacy policy.

items.title: OPES processor
items.text: SHOULD add its unique identification to the trace, with the uniqueness scope being the OPES System that contains it.

items.title: OPES service
items.text: MAY add its entry to the trace.

items.title: Delegation
items.text: An OPES entity MAY delegate the addition of its trace entry to another OPES entity.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE: A BYPASS REQUEST TRAVELLING BACK THROUGH THE FLOW

messages.label: BYPASS REQUEST
messages.note: The data consumer application sends a bypass instruction, usually embedded in an application message, naming the services to be bypassed by URI.

messages.label: BYPASS REQUEST
messages.note: The processor forwards the request to the next hop, which handles all bypass requests regardless of what the previous processor did.

messages.label: CONTENT
messages.note: If non-OPES content is available the named services are bypassed. If it is not, the request is ignored and the OPES version of the content is provided.
